mcqs.question: What exactly does a concurrent collection like ConcurrentHashMap guarantee?
options: That the entire application will never deadlock, regardless of other code
That every method it exposes runs in constant time regardless of size
That iteration order matches insertion order across all threads
That each individual method call is internally thread-safe — not that a sequence of calls your code makes is atomic together
mcqs.explanation: The guarantee is scoped to each individual call's internal correctness, not to any sequence of calls your own code builds on top. It says nothing about application-wide deadlocks, doesn't guarantee constant-time operations for every method, and doesn't promise insertion-order iteration.

mcqs.question: Why can two threads both insert a session for the same id despite using ConcurrentHashMap's containsKey and put?
options: containsKey and put are two separate calls; both threads can see containsKey return false before either calls put, so the second put silently overwrites the first
Because containsKey always returns false the first time it's called on any key
Because ConcurrentHashMap does not support the put() method
Because two threads can never call containsKey concurrently, only sequentially
mcqs.explanation: The check and the insert are two separate atomic calls with a gap between them where another thread can act — the classic check-then-act race, unaffected by the map being 'concurrent.' containsKey behaves normally, put is fully supported, and both methods can be called concurrently by multiple threads.

mcqs.question: What's a real cost of ConcurrentHashMap compared to a plain HashMap, even in single-threaded code?
options: ConcurrentHashMap requires a separate thread just to manage its internal locks
ConcurrentHashMap cannot store null keys or values, and does more internal bookkeeping than HashMap, which is unnecessary if there's no real concurrency
ConcurrentHashMap can only hold a maximum of 16 entries by default
ConcurrentHashMap's get() method always blocks, even for a single reader
mcqs.explanation: ConcurrentHashMap disallows null keys and values (unlike HashMap) and carries internal coordination overhead that buys nothing when only one thread ever accesses it. It uses no dedicated background thread, has no fixed 16-entry cap, and get() is non-blocking for readers.

mcqs.question: Why is wrapping every ConcurrentHashMap access in an external synchronized block a mistake?
options: It changes the map's iteration order unpredictably
It causes ConcurrentHashMap to throw an exception on the second synchronized call
It pays for both the map's own fine-grained internal locking and a coarse external lock, serializing access the map was designed to let proceed concurrently, for no benefit
It makes the map silently switch to a linked-list-based implementation
mcqs.explanation: The external lock forces every thread through one serialization point on top of the map's already-safe internal locking, throwing away the concurrency the map was built to provide. It doesn't affect iteration order, doesn't throw an exception, and doesn't change the map's implementation.
